On Saturn, that stable six‑sided meander rides around a warm polar vortex at the center, and because there’s no solid ground or mountains to break it up, the hexagon can persist for decades.

When scientists say the universe may be a hologram, they don’t mean we’re living in a sci‑fi projection. They mean something about how nature stores information. A hologram is a flat sheet that contains all the instructions to produce a 3D image. Likewise, the “holographic” idea suggests that everything happening in a volume of space could be fully described by information written on its boundary. Picture a snow globe: instead of listing every snowflake and swirl inside, all the data needed to reproduce the scene is etched on the glass. It’s a statement about bookkeeping, not about shadows on a wall—two different descriptions that carry the same content.

Why believe this wild-sounding idea? Black holes offer a clue. The amount of information you can stuff into a black hole grows with its surface area, not with the space inside, as if nature counts bits on the skin rather than in the bulk. That hint led to precise mathematical models where a world with gravity inside a region is exactly matched by a gravity-free theory living on the edge—a perfect translation between “inside” and “boundary” descriptions. This doesn’t say we’re in a computer simulation; it says the deepest laws might be simpler when written on a cosmic boundary. Whether or not our universe is truly holographic remains unproven, but even as a guiding principle it has sharpened our understanding of space, time, and how the pieces of physics fit together.

James Webb is now up and working, and it was built to do what Hubble can’t: see the universe in infrared, the glow of heat. Think of it as a time machine with night‑vision goggles. Its large, cold mirror and beach‑umbrella sunshield let it catch the faint warmth from the “baby pictures” of the cosmos—some of the first stars and galaxies that formed after the Big Bang. By using massive galaxy clusters as natural magnifying glasses, it can zoom in on tiny, distant galaxies and watch how the first city‑sized clumps of stars grew into today’s grand spirals and giants. It will also sharpen our measurements of how fast the universe is expanding, helping to settle disagreements left by earlier methods.

Closer to home, Webb is a dust‑piercing camera for cosmic weather and world‑building. It can look inside star‑forming clouds where new suns and planets are wrapped in blankets of dust, map the disks where planets are assembling, and read the “fingerprints” of chemicals like water, carbon dioxide, and methane in both those disks and in the atmospheres of planets around other stars—like sniffing the air of faraway worlds during a transit. In our own solar system, it studies the weather on the outer planets, the makeup of comets and icy moons, and the chemistry of the distant Kuiper Belt. In short, we expect Webb to reveal our universe’s childhood, its family album of forming stars and planets, and the ingredients that might make some distant worlds hospitable.

Yes—while depression has many causes, spending most of the day sitting does appear to nudge the odds upward. Large studies that follow people over time find that those who are more sedentary have about a 20–30% higher risk of developing depression, and those who move more—even modestly—have a 15–25% lower risk. Trials also show that adding regular physical activity can reduce depressive symptoms, especially in mild to moderate cases. Think of mind and body as sharing one battery: when the body never gets “discharged” through movement, the mental side can flicker.

Why would sitting so much matter? Movement acts like WD‑40 for the brain: it boosts mood chemicals, promotes growth factors that help nerve cells connect, lowers inflammation, steadies sleep-wake rhythms, and often brings sunlight and social contact. Long stretches of sitting, especially with passive screen time, can do the opposite—more rumination, poorer sleep, less daylight, less connection. The relationship is also two‑way: depression can make people less active, which then deepens low mood. The practical takeaway is not “become an athlete,” but “break up the stillness.” Short walks, standing up every hour, gentle chores, dancing to one song, or getting outside for daylight are small gears that turn bigger ones. Even light movement counts, and for many people it’s a safer first step than aiming for intense exercise.

Large creatures live life in the slow lane with big appetites. They need more food, more space, and more time to raise a small number of young. Picture an elephant’s pantry versus a rabbit’s: if a drought shrinks the pantry or a fence slices up the grocery store, the elephant runs into trouble sooner. Because big animals live at low densities—think of a few scattered lanterns across a dark landscape—losing even a handful can dim the whole species. And when numbers fall, recovery is slow; you can’t restock elephants or blue whales as quickly as mice.

Change and people also tilt the odds. We tend to target the biggest animals for meat, trophies, or fisheries, and roads and cities fragment the long routes they need to roam. Many large species sit near the top of long food chains; when the base wobbles, the top tips first, like a tall tower losing its lower bricks. Small, fast-reproducing creatures can pivot quickly to new conditions, but big ones are more like cargo ships—they turn slowly. This isn’t an iron rule—plenty of small species vanish too—but across history, from Ice Age megafauna to modern oceans, being large has often meant being fragile in a rapidly changing world.

Short answer: no, not in any practical sense. When light kicks electrons out of a bare, isolated piece of metal, the metal is left with a slight positive charge. That positive charge quickly acts like an electric “rubber band,” pulling back on the remaining electrons. After only a tiny number have escaped, this pull raises the “escape cost” so much that the incoming light can’t free any more. Emission largely stops long before you’ve removed a noticeable fraction of the metal’s electrons. Think of a few people slipping out of a stadium before security tightens the exits; soon, leaving becomes very hard.

If the metal is wired into a circuit, however, the wire supplies replacement electrons as fast as light kicks them out, so a steady flow (a current) can continue without the metal “running out.” And even then, the reservoir is enormous: a paperclip contains roughly 100 billion billion electrons. A modest photoelectric current of a microamp corresponds to about 6 trillion electrons per second; at that rate, draining every electron—if charging didn’t stop you and the metal didn’t get damaged—would take many centuries. In practice, stronger light just heats, melts, or even vaporizes the metal long before “electron depletion” becomes the limit. The real stoppers are charge buildup and material damage, not a shortage of electrons.

Imagine plucking a city commuter off their usual bus route and dropping them in an unfamiliar neighborhood with no phone. That’s roughly an ant’s situation. Ants navigate using a mix of “breadcrumb trails” (scent lines laid by other ants), a built‑in step counter, and a sun compass that helps them keep track of direction. If you move one to a strange spot, its internal “return‑home arrow” will point to where the nest should be based on its last walk, but because it’s been displaced, that arrow now leads to nowhere. After running out that mistaken route, the ant typically switches to a search pattern—looping and spiraling—while scanning for familiar smells, landmarks, and, most crucially, the colony’s scent trail.

What happens next depends on distance and species. If the ant is still within the colony’s foraging area, it may bump into a known trail or skyline and successfully plug back into the highway home. If it’s too far, time and luck run out: it may starve, be eaten, or be attacked if it meets ants from another colony, which recognize outsiders by their “team odor” and usually reject them. A few species that form vast, friendly supercolonies might tolerate a stranger with a similar scent, but that’s the exception. In short, a displaced ant will try its best navigator’s toolkit first, then comb the area for the colony’s “scent roads.” Reconnection is possible nearby; far away, the solitary worker is unlikely to make it back.

Think of your mouth like a small pond that keeps your teeth as stones on the shore. When the water gets too acidic, it slowly dissolves the stones—this is tooth decay. Moving the pond toward neutral or slightly basic helps minerals flow back into enamel, which is why saliva (a natural buffer) and mild alkaline helpers like baking-soda toothpaste can be protective. After acids from soda, juice, or frequent snacking, nudging pH back toward neutral (about 6.7–7.3) lowers the risk of cavities and helps enamel repair itself, especially with fluoride on board.

But push the pond too far the other way and new problems appear. In a very basic mouth, minerals can “fall out” of saliva and harden onto teeth as tartar (calculus)—a rough barnacle layer that traps plaque and irritates gums. A more alkaline environment can also favor bacteria that feed on proteins rather than sugars; they make sulfur gases (bad breath) and are linked to gum disease. Strong alkaline rinses can irritate cheeks and gums, too. The sweet spot is balance: limit frequent acidic drinks, sip water, chew sugar‑free gum to boost saliva, brush with fluoride (baking soda–containing pastes are fine), and avoid routine use of harsh alkaline solutions. If you battle lots of cavities or, conversely, heavy tartar, a dentist can check your saliva flow and pH and tailor advice.
